title: The Supreme Court's Other Docket
hook: The Court hears about sixty argued cases a year and disposes of thousands more by short written order. Most of what it does never gets an opinion at all.
key_points: Alongside the merits docket of argued cases, the Court issues orders — mostly one-line dispositions in lists released on scheduled order days.
The great majority are denials of certiorari, which set no precedent and say nothing about whether the decision below was right.
A 'GVR' — grant, vacate, remand — sends a case back for a lower court to reconsider in light of a new ruling, without the Court deciding it.
Occasionally the Court summarily reverses without argument, which is a real merits ruling delivered in a few pages.
Emergency applications, often called the shadow docket, are one part of this larger orders docket rather than the whole of it.
Writing at SCOTUSblog, Rory Little argues the orders docket matters far more than its low profile suggests, criminal cases especially.
content_html: Public attention tracks the Supreme Court's argued cases: briefs, oral argument, a signed opinion months later. That is roughly sixty decisions a year. The far larger stream is the orders docket — lists of short dispositions released on scheduled order days, resolving thousands of petitions with a line or two of text.
extra_html:
Most of those lines are denials of certiorari, which decide only that the Court will not hear a case; they set no precedent and imply no view of the merits. Others do real work. A GVR — grant, vacate, remand — erases a lower court's ruling and sends the case back to be reconsidered under a decision handed down since. A summary reversal decides a case outright without argument. And emergency applications, the ones usually labeled the shadow docket, are one part of this machinery rather than the whole of it.

Writing at SCOTUSblog, U.C. Law San Francisco professor Rory Little argues the orders docket deserves far more attention than it gets, and points to this term's criminal-law orders as a case in point: for a defendant, a one-line order can settle everything.

related.title: The Supreme Court's 'Shadow Docket'
related.hook: Most Supreme Court rulings today aren't fully-argued opinions — they're fast, often unsigned orders with little explanation. In the term ending October 2025, those quietly became the majority.

related.title: How the Supreme Court Decides a Case
related.hook: A top court hears only a sliver of the cases that beg for its attention — and the path from petition to ruling runs through written briefs, a public argument, and a vote taken in secret.

related.title: The One-Justice Order That Freezes a Case
related.hook: Before the Supreme Court decides anything, a single justice can push pause. That's how White House ballroom construction kept going after two lower courts had ordered it stopped.

related.title: When Federal Law Means Different Things in Different States
related.hook: Nine federal appeals courts have read the same detention statute; seven say one thing and two say the opposite. Until the Supreme Court steps in, your rights depend on your address.

flashcards.prompt: What does a denial of certiorari mean?

choices.text: The Court declined to hear the case — it sets no precedent and endorses nothing
The Court agreed with the lower court's reasoning
The lower court's ruling becomes binding nationwide

flashcards.explanation_html: Denials are the bulk of the orders docket. They leave the decision below standing in its own jurisdiction without approving it.

flashcards.back_html: Grant, vacate, remand — the Court wipes a lower ruling and sends the case back for reconsideration in light of a new decision, without deciding the case itself.

flashcards.prompt: How does the 'shadow docket' relate to the orders docket?
flashcards.back_html: Emergency applications are one slice of the much larger orders docket, which also covers cert denials, GVRs and summary dispositions.
